topics.title: Change and the meaning of a disaster

learn.hook: Mountains rise over millions of years; a flash flood rises in minutes. Nature changes at every speed, but we call some changes disasters.
points: Change is a continuous natural process. It varies in speed (fast or slow), magnitude and intensity: from the slow uplift of mountains to sudden earthquakes.
Nature treats change as value-neutral; it is humans who perceive changes as good or bad, desirable or undesirable, depending on how they affect us.
Activity idea: list environmental changes over long periods (e.g. formation of landforms, climate change) and short periods (e.g. floods, landslides), and classify them as desirable or undesirable.

A disaster is an undesirable occurrence resulting from forces largely beyond human control. It strikes quickly with little or no warning, causes or threatens serious disruption of life and property, including death and injury to many people, and needs efforts beyond those normally provided by statutory emergency services.

example.q: Is the slow formation of the Ganga delta over thousands of years a disaster? Is a cyclone that kills thousands in a day a disaster?
steps: A disaster strikes quickly and causes serious loss of life and property.
Delta formation is slow and gradual and creates fertile land → not a disaster.
The cyclone strikes suddenly with huge losses, needing large-scale relief → a disaster.
example.answer: Delta formation: not a disaster; the cyclone: a disaster.

learn.reallife: The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) is deployed when a calamity exceeds what local emergency services can handle.

quiz.explain: Humans, not nature, judge changes as good or bad.

Strikes quickly, causes serious losses and needs efforts beyond normal emergency services
quiz.explain: These features define a disaster.
quiz.mistake: Confuses disasters with slow natural change

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of slow environmental change?
quiz.explain: Landform formation takes very long periods.

quiz.q: Who perceives environmental changes as good or bad?
quiz.explain: Human perception gives value to changes.

quiz.q: A disaster requires mobilisation of efforts:
options: Beyond those normally provided by statutory emergency services
quiz.explain: Its scale exceeds normal emergency capacity.

quiz.q: A flood displaces 12,000 people; relief camps can hold 800 people each. How many camps are needed?

Assertion (A): The same natural change may be seen as useful by some and harmful by others.
Reason (R): Nature is value-neutral; humans judge changes by how they affect them.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Since value comes from human perception, judgements can differ.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What exactly is a disaster?'
teach.praise: Change is constant and value-neutral; a disaster strikes fast, causes huge losses and overwhelms normal services. Gappu understands disasters!
teach.nudge: Explain how change and disaster differ and give the features of a disaster.

topics.title: Human-made disasters, hazards and changing patterns

learn.hook: The 1984 Bhopal gas tragedy shows that disasters are not only natural. Some are made by human mistakes.
points: Some disasters are human-induced: the Bhopal gas tragedy, the Chernobyl nuclear disaster, wars, release of CFCs and greenhouse gases, and environmental pollution (noise, air, water and soil).
Some human activities indirectly intensify disasters: deforestation, unscientific land use and construction in fragile areas can trigger landslides and floods.
Human-made disasters can, to an extent, be prevented; natural disasters cannot be prevented but can be mitigated and managed.

A natural hazard is an element of circumstances in the natural environment that has the potential to cause harm to people, property or both, e.g. ocean currents, steep slopes and unstable structures in the Himalaya, or extreme conditions in deserts and glaciated areas. A hazard becomes a disaster when it actually strikes and causes large losses.

Disasters are becoming more frequent and larger in magnitude. One reason is that, with technology, people increasingly settle in hazard-prone areas such as floodplains, steep slopes and coasts, so perceptions and patterns of disasters have changed.

example.q: Is a steep, unstable Himalayan slope a hazard or a disaster? What if it collapses onto a village?
steps: A hazard is a natural condition with potential to cause harm.
The unstable slope is a hazard.
When it collapses and kills people or destroys property, it becomes a disaster.
example.answer: The slope is a hazard; the collapse affecting the village is a disaster.

learn.reallife: Unplanned construction on steep slopes in hill towns has been linked to worse landslide damage during heavy monsoon rains.

games.title: Hazard or disaster?

quiz.explain: Mitigation and management reduce their impact.

quiz.q: One reason disasters are causing larger losses today is that people:
quiz.explain: Technology lets people occupy floodplains, slopes and coasts, raising exposure.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of a natural hazard mentioned by NCERT?
options: Steep slopes and unstable structures in the Himalaya
quiz.explain: Such slopes have the potential to cause harm.

quiz.q: A district had 4 major floods in one decade and 10 in the next. By how many did the number increase?

Reason (R): Every hazard automatically turns into a disaster sooner or later.

Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: a hazard is only a potential threat; it becomes a disaster only when it actually strikes and causes large losses to people and property.

teach.nudge: Explain human-made disasters, what a hazard is and why disasters are increasing.

topics.title: International efforts: Yokohama Strategy and IDNDR

learn.hook: Disasters cross borders, so countries came together in Yokohama, Japan, in 1994 to plan a 'Safer World'.
points: Important milestones in disaster management include the establishment of the National Institute of Disaster Management in India, the Earth Summit at Rio de Janeiro (1992) and the World Conference on Disaster Management at Yokohama, Japan (May 1994).

The UN General Assembly in 1989 took up natural disaster reduction, leading to the 'Yokohama Strategy and Plan of Action for a Safer World' in 1994. The decade 1990–2000 was declared the International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction (IDNDR).

The World Conference on Natural Disaster Reduction was held at Yokohama, Japan, from 23 to 27 May 1994. It recognised that human and economic losses from disasters are rising and that poor and developing countries are hit hardest.
Each country has the sovereign responsibility to protect its citizens from natural disasters. Priority should be given to developing, least developed, land-locked and small island developing states.
Countries should develop and strengthen national capacities and legislation, and promote regional and international cooperation for capacity building, technology sharing and mobilising resources.

example.q: How many days did the Yokohama World Conference last, from 23 to 27 May 1994 inclusive?
steps: Counting both the first and last days: 4 + 1 = 5.

learn.reallife: India's National Institute of Disaster Management in New Delhi trains officials in planning and response, building national capacity as Yokohama urged.

topics.title: Classification of natural disasters and India's vulnerability

learn.hook: Locust swarms, cold waves, avalanches and tsunamis are all natural disasters, but they come from very different parts of the earth system.
points: Natural disasters are classified into four categories: atmospheric, terrestrial, aquatic and biological.
Atmospheric: blizzards, thunderstorms, lightning, tornadoes, tropical cyclones, droughts, hailstorms, frost, heat waves or loo, and cold waves.
Terrestrial: earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides, avalanches, subsidence and soil erosion.

Aquatic: floods, tidal waves, ocean currents, storm surges and tsunamis. Biological: plants and animals as colonisers (e.g. locusts), and insect infestation and fungal, bacterial and viral diseases such as bird flu and dengue.

India is highly vulnerable to disasters because of its large size, great physical diversity, unique geo-climatic conditions and very large population; social and economic inequalities can make some groups even more vulnerable.

example.q: Classify: (a) heat wave in Rajasthan; (b) avalanche in Kashmir; (c) storm surge in Odisha; (d) locust attack in Gujarat.
steps: (a) Heat wave → atmospheric.
(b) Avalanche → terrestrial.
(c) Storm surge → aquatic.
(d) Locusts → biological.

learn.reallife: The 2020 locust swarms that damaged crops in Rajasthan and Gujarat were a biological disaster.

quiz.q: Natural disasters are classified into how many categories?
quiz.explain: Atmospheric, terrestrial, aquatic and biological.

quiz.q: A blizzard is classified as a/an:
quiz.explain: Blizzards are atmospheric.

quiz.q: Which of these is a terrestrial disaster?
quiz.explain: Avalanches, earthquakes and landslides are terrestrial.
quiz.mistake: Picks an aquatic or atmospheric disaster

quiz.q: A tsunami is classified as a/an:
quiz.explain: Tsunamis are listed under aquatic disasters.

quiz.q: Locust swarms and dengue outbreaks are:
quiz.explain: They involve living organisms.

quiz.q: Heat wave or loo is classified as:
quiz.explain: It is an atmospheric disaster.
quiz.mistake: Thinks heat affects land so it is terrestrial

quiz.q: If a state recorded 3 atmospheric, 2 terrestrial and 4 aquatic disasters in a year, how many disasters is that in total?

Assertion (A): India is highly vulnerable to natural disasters.
Reason (R): India's large size, physical diversity and large population expose many people to many kinds of hazards.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Varied hazards over a large, populous country raise vulnerability.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How are natural disasters grouped?'
teach.praise: Atmospheric, terrestrial, aquatic and biological disasters, and why India is so vulnerable. Gappu has the full list!
teach.nudge: Name the four categories with examples and explain India's vulnerability.

topics.title: Earthquakes in India: causes, regions and zones

learn.hook: The Indian plate creeps north by about a centimetre a year. That tiny push builds enormous stress along the Himalaya.
points: Earthquakes are among the most unpredictable and highly destructive natural disasters. Those of tectonic origin are the most devastating and widespread.

The Indian plate is moving about 1 cm per year towards the north and north-east. This movement is constantly obstructed by the Eurasian plate, so stress builds up and is released as earthquakes, especially along the Himalayan arc.
The most vulnerable regions are Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, the Darjeeling subdivision of West Bengal and all the north-eastern states.

Central-western India has also had damaging earthquakes: Gujarat (1819, 1956 and 2001) and Maharashtra (1967 and 1993). The 1993 quake hit Latur and Osmanabad, along the Bhima (Krishna) fault, within the supposedly stable Peninsular block.

India is divided into five earthquake zones: very high damage risk, high damage risk, moderate damage risk, low damage risk and very low damage risk zones. Map reading: identify these zones on the earthquake hazard map of India.

example.q: At about 1 cm per year, how far will the Indian plate move in 10,000 years (in metres)?
steps: Distance = 1 cm × 10,000 = 10,000 cm.

learn.reallife: Building codes from the Bureau of Indian Standards require stronger, earthquake-resistant designs in the higher-risk seismic zones of India.

quiz.q: The Indian plate is moving at about how much per year towards the north and north-east?
quiz.explain: NCERT gives about 1 cm per year.

quiz.q: Earthquakes along the Himalayan arc result mainly from:
options: Stress built up as the Eurasian plate obstructs the northward-moving Indian plate
quiz.explain: Plate collision builds and releases stress.

quiz.q: Which of these is among the most earthquake-vulnerable regions of India?
quiz.explain: The North-East lies along active plate margins.

quiz.q: The 1993 earthquake in Latur and Osmanabad occurred along the:
quiz.explain: NCERT links it with the Bhima (Krishna) fault.

quiz.q: Gujarat experienced damaging earthquakes in:
quiz.explain: NCERT lists 1819, 1956 and 2001 for Gujarat.

quiz.q: India is divided into how many earthquake damage risk zones?
quiz.explain: Very high, high, moderate, low and very low.

quiz.q: How many years passed between the Gujarat earthquakes of 1956 and 2001?

Assertion (A): Earthquakes can occur even in the Peninsular block, which is considered stable.
Reason (R): India is divided into five earthquake damage risk zones.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the number of risk zones does not explain Peninsular earthquakes. They occur because faults in the Peninsula, such as the Bhima (Krishna) fault behind the 1993 Latur quake, can still be active.
quiz.mistake: Marks (a) whenever both statements are true without checking the link

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why are earthquakes common in the Himalaya, and where else do they occur in India?'
teach.praise: A 1 cm-per-year push against Eurasia, risky Himalayan and north-eastern belts, quakes in Gujarat and Latur, and five risk zones. Gappu is quake-aware!
teach.nudge: Explain the cause of Indian earthquakes, the vulnerable regions and the five zones.

learn.hook: Earthquakes rarely kill by shaking alone. It is collapsing buildings that cause most deaths, which is why safer construction saves lives.
points: Socio-environmental consequences: earthquakes destroy lives and property, settlements, infrastructure, transport and communication, industries and historical and cultural monuments; they can wipe out whole towns in moments.
Effects on the ground (NCERT table): fissures, settlements, landslides, liquefaction and earth pressure, possibly with chain reactions.
Effects on man-made structures: cracking, sliding, overturning, buckling and collapse. Effects on water: waves, hydro-dynamic pressure and tsunami.

Mitigation: (i) establish seismological centres for regular monitoring and fast dissemination of information; GPS can help monitor plate movement. (ii) Prepare a vulnerability map of the country and spread risk information, educating people on how to reduce impacts.

(iii) Modify house types and building designs in vulnerable areas and discourage high-rise buildings, large industrial establishments and big urban centres there. (iv) Make earthquake-resistant designs mandatory and use light materials in major construction in vulnerable areas.

example.q: Why are light building materials recommended in earthquake-prone areas?
steps: During shaking, heavy materials (stone, concrete roofs) fall with great force.
Falling heavy debris causes most injuries and deaths.
Light materials cause less damage if they fall.
So light materials reduce casualties.
example.answer: Because light materials cause less harm if structures fail during shaking.

learn.reallife: Traditional Assam-type houses with light bamboo and timber walls have long been considered safer in the earthquake-prone North-East.

quiz.q: Which of these is an effect of earthquakes on water?

quiz.explain: Resistant designs and light materials reduce damage.

quiz.explain: GPS tracks small shifts in the earth's crust.

options: High-rise buildings, large industries and big urban centres
quiz.explain: These increase exposure to earthquake damage.

quiz.explain: Fissures, settlements, landslides, liquefaction and earth pressure affect the ground.

quiz.mistake: Gives the number of safe buildings

Assertion (A): Preparing a vulnerability map helps reduce earthquake losses.
Reason (R): It helps spread risk information and educate people about reducing adverse impacts.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A

quiz.explain: Knowing where risk is high lets people and planners prepare.

teach.praise: Ground, structure and water effects, and mitigation through monitoring, mapping and safer buildings. Gappu is building safely!

learn.hook: On 26 December 2004, a massive undersea earthquake near Sumatra sent walls of water across the Indian Ocean, reaching the coasts of Tamil Nadu and the Andamans within hours.
points: A tsunami (also called a harbour wave or seismic sea wave) is a series of high waves caused when earthquakes or volcanic eruptions make the sea floor move abruptly, suddenly displacing ocean water.
In the deep ocean, a tsunami has a very long wavelength and limited wave height, so ships at sea are hardly affected and tsunamis are difficult to detect there.

A tsunami's speed depends on the depth of water: it races across the deep ocean at several hundred km/h, and as it approaches a shallow coast it slows down while its height rises, reaching 15 m or more, causing large-scale destruction of coastal settlements.

Tsunamis are frequently observed along the Pacific Ring of Fire, especially along the coasts of Alaska, Japan, the Philippines and other islands of South-east Asia, Indonesia, and also in the Indian Ocean. They cause the most damage on densely populated coasts.

The Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004 killed well over 2 lakh people across many countries (NCERT puts the toll at over 3 lakh; most later counts give about 2.3 lakh). After it, India joined the International Tsunami Warning System. Because losses are so large and widespread, mitigating tsunamis needs international cooperation.

example.q: Why can a ship in the open ocean ride over a tsunami without noticing it?
steps: In deep water, a tsunami's wavelength is very long.
Its height there is small.
So the sea surface rises only slightly and gradually under the ship.
The wave grows tall only near shallow coasts.
example.answer: Because in deep water the tsunami is a long, low wave.

learn.reallife: INCOIS in Hyderabad runs the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre, set up after 2004, which can issue alerts within minutes of an undersea quake.

learn.hook: A cyclone is a giant heat engine: it drinks warm sea water as vapour, releases its heat in towering clouds, and spins with winds averaging about 180 km/h at India's coasts.
points: Tropical cyclones are intense low-pressure areas between 30°N and 30°S, around which high-velocity winds blow. Horizontally they extend 500–1,000 km and vertically from the surface to 12–14 km.
A tropical cyclone is like a heat engine energised by latent heat released when moisture gathered over warm oceans condenses.

Initial conditions: (i) large, continuous supply of warm, moist air; (ii) strong Coriolis force to prevent filling of the central low (its absence near the equator prevents cyclones between 0° and 5°); (iii) unstable conditions through the troposphere; (iv) absence of strong vertical wind shear, which would disturb vertical transport of latent heat. Structure: a calm eye with clear sky, surrounded by an eye wall of spirally rising winds.

In India, cyclones originate in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea. Most originate between 10° and 15°N during the monsoon season; in the Bay of Bengal they mostly develop in October and November, and their place of origin shifts with the seasons.

Since cyclones draw energy from the sea, their force decreases with distance from it after landfall. Coastal areas are most vulnerable, struck by winds averaging about 180 km/h, often with a storm surge (abnormal rise in sea level) that floods settlements and fields. Map reading: wind and cyclone hazard zones of India.

example.q: Why do cyclones not form between 0° and 5° latitude?
steps: Cyclones need a strong Coriolis force to keep the central low from filling up.
The Coriolis force is absent at the equator and very weak near it.
Without it, air flows straight into the low.
So no cyclone develops between 0° and 5°.
example.answer: Because the Coriolis force is absent or too weak near the equator.

learn.reallife: Odisha's network of cyclone shelters and early evacuation greatly reduced deaths in cyclones like Phailin (2013) and Fani (2019).

games.title: Condition for cyclone formation?
items: Continuous supply of warm, moist air

quiz.explain: NCERT gives 30°N–30°S.

quiz.q: The energy of a tropical cyclone comes from:
quiz.explain: It is a heat engine powered by condensation.

options: The Coriolis force is absent near the equator
quiz.explain: Without Coriolis, the low fills up instead of spinning.

quiz.q: The calm centre of a cyclone with clear sky is the:
quiz.explain: The eye is calm; strong winds are in the eye wall.

quiz.q: Strong vertical wind shear is unfavourable for cyclones because it:
options: Disturbs the vertical transport of latent heat
quiz.explain: Shear tears apart the cyclone's heat engine.

quiz.q: An abnormal rise in sea level caused by a cyclone is called a:
quiz.explain: Cyclone winds push water ashore as a storm surge.

quiz.q: A cyclone moves at 15 km/h towards a coast 270 km away. How many hours until landfall?

Assertion (A): Tropical cyclones grow stronger as they move inland after landfall.
Reason (R): Tropical cyclones draw their energy from warm, moist air over the sea.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: cyclones weaken after landfall. R is true, and it explains why: over land, their supply of moisture and latent heat is cut off.

quiz.explain: NCERT notes that most cyclones originate between 10° and 15°N during the monsoon. None form between 0° and 5° because the Coriolis force is too weak there.

learn.hook: Every monsoon, the Brahmaputra and Kosi spill over vast areas, while desert towns in Rajasthan sometimes face sudden flash floods.
points: A flood is the inundation of land and human settlements when water in river channels rises and spills over, usually when surface runoff exceeds the carrying capacity of channels and flows into low-lying floodplains.

Natural causes: intense rainfall, storm surges, prolonged rain, melting of ice and snow, reduced infiltration and a high load of eroded material. Human causes: indiscriminate deforestation, unscientific agricultural practices, disturbance of natural drainage channels and colonisation of floodplains and river beds.
Floods are common in China, India and Bangladesh. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog (National Flood Commission) identified 40 million hectares of land in India as flood-prone.

Assam, West Bengal and Bihar are among the most flood-prone states. Rivers of Punjab and Uttar Pradesh also flood occasionally. Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana and Punjab increasingly face flash floods, partly due to the monsoon pattern and partly due to human blocking of streams and channels. Tamil Nadu sometimes floods in November–January due to the retreating monsoon.

Contrast: floods in eastern India (Assam, Bihar, West Bengal) are frequent and widespread, caused by heavy monsoon rain, huge sediment loads and large Himalayan rivers; floods in western states are more often sudden flash floods linked with intense rain and blocked drainage. Map reading: flood hazard zones of India.

example.q: Why are Assam and Bihar among the most flood-prone states?
steps: They receive heavy monsoon rainfall.
Large Himalayan rivers like the Brahmaputra and Kosi carry huge sediment loads.
Sediment raises river beds, reducing channel capacity.
So rivers frequently overflow onto the plains.
example.answer: Heavy rain plus large, sediment-laden Himalayan rivers overflowing their channels.

learn.reallife: The Central Water Commission issues flood forecasts for hundreds of river stations, helping districts in Assam and Bihar evacuate in time.

learn.hook: Floods can destroy crops and homes, yet on Majuli island in Assam, the yearly floods also leave behind fresh silt that grows excellent paddy.
points: Consequences: frequent inundation of farmland and settlements damages crops, roads, rails, bridges and houses; people and cattle are displaced, and economies suffer.
After floods, water-borne diseases such as cholera, gastro-enteritis and hepatitis spread.
Benefits: floods deposit fertile silt on farmland every year. Majuli in Assam, the largest riverine island in the world, gives good paddy crops after the annual Brahmaputra floods.
Control measures: building flood-protection embankments, constructing dams, afforestation, and discouraging major construction in the upper reaches of rivers.
Removing human encroachment from river channels and depopulating floodplains help reduce losses; in coastal areas prone to cyclonic floods, cyclone centres provide shelter.

example.q: Give one harm and one benefit of annual floods in the Brahmaputra valley.
steps: Harm: crops, houses, roads and bridges are damaged and people are displaced.
Benefit: fresh fertile silt is deposited, giving good paddy crops, as on Majuli.
example.answer: Harm: damage and displacement; benefit: fertile silt for paddy.

topics.title: Droughts: meaning, types and drought-prone areas

learn.hook: Jaisalmer and Barmer get less than 90 mm of rain a year on average. For them, drought is not an event but a constant threat.
points: A drought is an extended period of shortage of water availability due to inadequate precipitation, excessive evaporation and over-use of water from reservoirs and other stores, including groundwater. It is a complex phenomenon involving meteorological, hydrological, agricultural, socio-economic and ecological elements.

Types: (i) meteorological drought: a prolonged period of inadequate rainfall, poorly distributed in time and space; (ii) agricultural drought (soil moisture drought): low soil moisture causes crop failure; an area with more than 30% of its gross cropped area irrigated is excluded from the drought-prone category; (iii) hydrological drought: water in aquifers, lakes and reservoirs falls below what precipitation can replenish; (iv) ecological drought: productivity of a natural ecosystem fails due to water shortage.
About 19% of India's area and 12% of its population suffer from drought every year. About 30% of the country's area is drought-prone, affecting around 50 million people.

Extreme drought: most of Rajasthan west of the Aravali (Marusthali) and the Kachchh region of Gujarat; districts like Jaisalmer and Barmer receive less than 90 mm average annual rainfall. Severe drought: parts of eastern Rajasthan, most of Madhya Pradesh, eastern Maharashtra, interior Andhra Pradesh and the Karnataka plateau, northern interior Tamil Nadu, southern Jharkhand and interior Odisha.

Moderate drought: northern Rajasthan, Haryana, southern Uttar Pradesh, the rest of Gujarat, Maharashtra except Konkan, Jharkhand, the Coimbatore plateau of Tamil Nadu and interior Karnataka. Droughts are frequent in central and western India because rainfall there is low and highly variable and many areas lie in rain shadows. Map reading: drought-prone areas of India.

example.q: A district has 40% of its gross cropped area irrigated. Is it in the drought-prone category for agricultural drought?
steps: Areas with more than 30% of gross cropped area under irrigation are excluded.
40% is more than 30%.
So it is excluded from the drought-prone category.
example.answer: No, it is excluded because irrigation exceeds 30%.

learn.reallife: MGNREGA works like farm ponds and check dams are often prioritised in drought-prone districts of Maharashtra and Rajasthan.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is a drought, and where in India is it common?'
teach.praise: Water shortage of four types, 30% of India drought-prone, extreme in Marusthali and Kachchh. Gappu is drought-aware!
teach.nudge: Define drought, name its four types and give the extreme and severe drought areas.

learn.hook: Rajasthan's villagers have words for the worst droughts: akal for food, jalkal for water, trinkal for fodder, and trikal when all three fail together.
points: Consequences: crop failure causes scarcity of food grains (akal) and fodder (trinkal); inadequate rainfall causes shortage of water (jalkal); shortage of all three, trikal, is the most devastating.

Droughts cause large-scale death of cattle and other animals, migration of people and livestock, and spread of water-borne diseases (gastro-enteritis, cholera, hepatitis) when people are forced to drink contaminated water.
Short-term mitigation: provide safe drinking water, medicines for victims, fodder and water for cattle, and shift people and livestock to safer places.

Long-term mitigation: identify groundwater potential (aquifers), transfer river water from surplus to deficit areas, plan inter-linking of rivers, build reservoirs and dams, promote drought-resistant crops, and practise rainwater harvesting.
Remote sensing and satellite imagery help identify river basins that can be inter-linked and areas with groundwater potential.

example.q: Classify these drought measures as short-term or long-term: (a) tankers supplying drinking water; (b) rooftop rainwater harvesting; (c) shifting cattle to fodder camps; (d) growing drought-resistant crops.
steps: Immediate relief → short-term: (a), (c).
Lasting solutions → long-term: (b), (d).

learn.reallife: Rooftop rainwater harvesting is compulsory for new buildings in many Indian cities, such as Chennai, to recharge groundwater.

learn.hook: In August 1998, a massive landslide at Malpa in Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand, buried a village and a group of Kailash Mansarovar pilgrims.
points: A landslide is the rapid sliding of a large mass of bedrock or debris down a slope. Landslides are highly localised, controlled by geology, geomorphic agents, slope, land use, vegetation cover and human activities, so they are difficult and costly to monitor and predict.

Very high vulnerability zone: highly unstable, young mountainous areas of the Himalaya and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, high-rainfall steep slopes of the Western Ghats and Nilgiris, the north-eastern regions, earthquake-prone areas and areas of intense construction (roads, dams).
High vulnerability zone: areas with similar conditions but a different combination, intensity and frequency of factors; all Himalayan states and north-eastern states except the plains of Assam.

Moderate to low vulnerability: low-precipitation Trans-Himalayan Ladakh and Spiti, the stable Aravali, rain-shadow areas of the Western and Eastern Ghats and the Deccan; mining and subsidence areas in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, MP, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Goa and Kerala. Other (safe) areas: Rajasthan, Haryana, UP, Bihar, West Bengal (except Darjeeling), Assam (except Karbi Anglong) and coastal regions of southern states.

Consequences: roadblocks, destruction of railway lines, and blocking of river channels by rock falls (which can cause floods), making movement risky and costly. Mitigation: restrict construction and settlements in vulnerable zones; limit agriculture to valleys and moderate slopes; large-scale afforestation; bunds to reduce water flow; and terrace farming instead of jhumming in north-eastern hill states. Project idea: a case study of the Malpa landslide.

example.q: Why is terrace farming recommended instead of jhumming on north-eastern hill slopes?
steps: Jhumming clears and burns forest on slopes, leaving soil loose.
Loose soil on steep slopes slides easily in heavy rain.
Terraces break the slope into steps and hold soil and water.
So terracing reduces landslides.
example.answer: Because terraces stabilise slopes, while jhum clearing loosens them.

learn.reallife: The Border Roads Organisation constantly clears landslides on highways to Sikkim, Arunachal and Uttarakhand during the monsoon.

learn.hook: In 1999, the Odisha super cyclone killed about 10,000 people. In 2019, the very strong Cyclone Fani hit the same coast, but large-scale planned evacuation kept deaths far lower. Management makes the difference.
points: Cyclones are relatively easier to manage because they are more predictable in time and place. Measures include cyclone shelters, embankments, dykes, reservoirs and afforestation to reduce wind speed.
Losses from cyclones are higher in India, Bangladesh and Myanmar because of dense populations in coastal areas.

The Disaster Management Act, 2005 defines a disaster as a catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence in any area, arising from natural or man-made causes, or by accident or negligence, which results in substantial loss of life or human suffering or damage to property or the environment, and is beyond the coping capacity of the affected community.

Disaster management has three stages: (i) pre-disaster: generating data and information, preparing vulnerability zoning maps, spreading awareness, disaster planning, preparedness and preventive measures; (ii) during disaster: rescue and relief operations such as evacuation, shelters and relief camps, and supply of water, food, clothing and medical care; (iii) post-disaster: rehabilitation and recovery of victims and capacity building.

A large part of India's area and population is vulnerable to disasters, so mitigation and preparedness are the best options. Project ideas: reports on the Malpa landslide, the 2004 tsunami, the Odisha and Gujarat cyclones, river inter-linking, the Tehri or Sardar Sarovar dam, the Bhuj or Latur earthquakes, life in a delta, or a rooftop rainwater harvesting model.

example.q: Place each action in the right stage: (a) preparing a flood vulnerability map; (b) evacuating people by boat; (c) rebuilding houses with flood-resistant designs.
steps: (a) Planning before the event → pre-disaster.
(b) Rescue during the event → during disaster.
(c) Rehabilitation and capacity building afterwards → post-disaster.

learn.reallife: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and state authorities run mock drills in schools, part of pre-disaster preparedness.
